claims.text: Protective-scale development in HEAs is governed by selective surface segregation and controlled oxidation of reactive elements such as Al or Cr.
Sluggish diffusion and severe lattice distortion in HEAs cause formation of a continuous, dense, and adherent protective oxide layer.
A sufficient concentration of Al or Cr enables protective-oxide formation, whereas a deficient concentration does not.
Reactive-element concentration can be varied while other relevant alloy and test factors are held constant to isolate its effect.
Exposure at 1000–1100 °C for as long as 200 hours can reveal both oxide formation and long-term scale stability.
The reactive element segregates to the alloy surface during high-temperature oxidation.
An Al2O3- or Cr-containing adherent oxide scale acts as a diffusion barrier.
Sluggish diffusion in the HEA prevents rapid depletion of the reactive element from the bulk.
The reactive element's high oxygen affinity promotes its selective oxidation after it reaches the surface.
A dense protective oxide slows oxidation by inhibiting oxygen ingress and metal-ion diffusion.
The variant with adequate reactive-element content will form a continuous protective scale with parabolic growth kinetics that persists during prolonged exposure.
The high-reactive-element variant will have significantly lower mass gain than the low-reactive-element variant.
An alloy deficient in the protective reactive element will form a discontinuous or non-protective oxide scale.
The deficient alloy will exhibit linear or exponential oxidation kinetics and higher mass gain.

The proposed mechanism applies primarily to multi-principal-element alloys in which high entropy, sluggish diffusion, and lattice distortion are significant, under oxidizing conditions above about 1000 °C.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to simpler alloys or to milder oxidative environments.
The threshold reactive-element concentration needed to form a protective scale is not yet quantified.
The unique contribution of HEA-induced sluggish diffusion to scale adherence and renewal relative to conventional alloys remains unquantified.
Mass-change measurements, XRD, and SEM/EDS can distinguish oxidation kinetics, oxide phases, scale continuity, and scale composition.

The hypothesis would be falsified if the high- and low-reactive-element variants showed no significant difference in oxidation rate, scale thickness, or scale continuity and the high-content variant failed to form a protective scale.
